query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high‐entropy alloys (HEAs) designed for high‐temperature applications, the intrinsic high configurational entropy promotes a kinetically favorable surface segregation of oxide‐forming elements (such as aluminum) that rapidly nucleates and sustains a continuous, adherent protective oxide scale, thereby enhancing oxidation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenized HEA containing multiple principal elements with a baseline balanced level of oxide‐forming elements (e.g., Al) suitable for high-temperature exposure.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the concentration of a key oxide‐forming element (e.g., aluminum) in otherwise compositionally equivalent HEA samples.
generation.conditions: Expose the alloys to high-temperature oxidation conditions (e.g., 850–1100 °C in an air or oxidizing atmosphere) while monitoring surface composition evolution in situ using techniques such as XPS or ToF-SIMS.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced surface enrichment of the oxide-forming element that facilitates the nucleation and continuity of a protective oxide layer.
generation.mechanism: The high configurational entropy decreases the energetic barrier for the diffusion and segregation of oxide‐forming elements to the surface. Once enriched at the surface, these elements react with oxygen to form a dense, adherent oxide scale that acts as a barrier to further oxygen diffusion and overall alloy oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with increased concentrations of the selected oxide‐forming element will form a protective oxide scale more rapidly and exhibit reduced oxidation rates (i.e., lower weight gain over time) compared to the baseline alloy with lower concentration.
generation.baseline: An HEA with a standard (balanced) concentration of the oxide‐forming element, displaying typical oxidation behavior without accelerated surface-enrichment.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for multi-principal element alloys exposed to high enough temperatures to activate diffusion but below temperatures where severe scale spallation or bulk alloy degradation dominates. It may not apply under non-oxidizing conditions or in alloys with extreme deviations in overall composition.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative relationship between the concentration of the oxide-former and the kinetics of protective layer formation, as well as potential inter-element interactions affecting diffusivity, remain to be fully defined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples that are identical in all aspects except for the concentration of the key oxide-forming element (e.g., one set with enhanced Al content and one with baseline levels). Subject both to the same high-temperature oxidation environment with real-time surface composition monitoring.
measurements: Temporal weight gain to monitor overall oxidation rate
In situ surface analysis (e.g., XPS or ToF-SIMS) to track the segregation of the oxide-forming element
Microscopic characterization (e.g., SEM/EDS) of the oxide scale morphology, thickness, and adherence
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no statistically significant difference in the rate, continuity, or protective quality of the oxide scale is observed between the enhanced and baseline samples, or if the oxide-forming element does not exhibit preferential surface segregation in the enhanced sample, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. Abstract A novel metal matrix composite based on the NbMoCrTiAl high entropy alloy (HEA) was designed by the in-situ formation method. The microstructure, phase evolution, and compression mechanical properties at room temperature of the composite are investigated in detail. The results confirmed that the composite was primarily composed of body-centered cubic solid solution with a small amount of titanium carbides and alumina. With the presence of approximately 7.0 vol. % Al 2 O 3 and 32.2 vol. % TiC reinforced particles, the compressive fracture strength of the composite (1542 MPa) was increased by approximately 50% compared with that of the as-cast NbMoCrTiAl HEA. In consideration of the superior oxidation resistance, the P/M NbMoCrTiAl high entropy alloy composite could be considered as a promising high temperature structural material. Keywords: high entropy alloys, metal matrix composites, mechanical properties

Abstract This work investigates the effect of ultrafine-grain microstructure on the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA). The ultrafine-grain microstructure is obtained using stationary friction processing performed at two different rotational speeds, 400 and 1800 rpm, for 5 min duration. Processed samples demonstrate high depth of refinement (DOR) and ultrafine grain size (0.43–1 μm) at high rotational speeds along with significant phase transformations from BCC/B2 to FCC microstructure. Further, surface free energy of the ultrafine-grain microstructure is enhanced up to 35%. Oxidation kinetics of the ultrafine-grained sample is decelerated up to 12–48% in a temperature range of 850–1050 °C for a duration of 100 h. Chromia and alumina were the predominant oxides formed in almost all the samples oxidized at elevated temperature. In addition, spinel Co(Cr,Fe) 2 O 4 /Fe(Co,Cr) 2 O 4 formation is also detected in the unprocessed oxidized samples. Processed samples rich in grain boundaries (GBs) promote internal oxidation to form Al-rich inner oxides. decision.trend: Early studies on high‐entropy and refractory alloys under high‐temperature oxidation conditions (PMC6317005) identified that the oxide scale and its kinetics vary drastically with temperature and composition, revealing that oxide‐forming elements may not always produce a protective layer. Later work (PMC10142552) demonstrated that intentional variations in composition (e.g., altering Cr content) impact the oxide formation, hinting that the balance of element segregation and oxide kinetics plays a key role. More recently, in situ studies (PMC10384371) have tracked how oxidation proceeds in complex HEAs, showing that even though individual elements oxidize at different rates, a clear mechanistic model linking preferential surface enrichment and continuous oxide scale formation remains missing.
decision.unsolved: It remains unresolved whether the intrinsic high configurational entropy in HEAs actually drives a kinetically favorable segregation of high oxide-forming elements (such as Al or Cr) that in turn governs the formation and retention of a protective, adherent oxide layer. In particular, the quantitative relationship between the rate of surface enrichment (versus bulk diffusion) and the emergence of a continuous, protective oxide scale under aggressive, high‐temperature oxidation conditions needs to be isolated and directly tested.
decision.lever: Systematically vary the concentration of a key oxide-forming component (e.g., Al or Cr) in an otherwise compositionally equivalent HEA, combined with in situ surface analysis (such as XPS or ToF-SIMS) during oxidation tests at high temperature.
decision.why: Because the trend shows that previous experiments altered compositions and observed differences in oxidation behavior without isolating surface segregation kinetics, a controlled variable experiment targeting only the level of the oxide-former will allow researchers to directly determine if a faster or enhanced surface enrichment is responsible for developing and retaining the protective oxide layer. This lever isolates the segregation mechanism, providing a clear controlled comparison relative to a baseline alloy, and offers a definitive path to falsification if no significant difference in protective oxide formation is observed.
